report:
## Conclusion

The claim is **supported by strong evidence**. Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation before cesarean delivery modestly but consistently reduces surgical-site infection (SSI) compared with iodine-based preparations (with or without alcohol).

The pivotal evidence is a large, well-designed multicenter randomized trial (Tuuli et al., NEJM 2016) of over 1,700 women undergoing cesarean delivery, which found chlorhexidine-alcohol significantly reduced SSI risk compared with iodine-alcohol (relative risk ~0.55, roughly halving infection rates) (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048). Smaller individual RCTs have shown mixed statistical significance—some, like a pilot trial in India, found a lower but non-statistically-significant SSI rate with chlorhexidine (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8369632/)—but pooled analyses are more definitive.

The Cochrane systematic review (Hadiati et al., 2020), the most authoritative synthesis of RCT data, concluded that chlorhexidine gluconate skin preparation before cesarean section is "probably slightly more effective" at reducing SSI compared with povidone-iodine, based on moderate-certainty evidence (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD007462.pub5/full). This is consistent with a separate meta-analysis (Kunkle et al., 2019) reporting reduced SSI with chlorhexidine-alcohol versus povidone-iodine across pooled cesarean trials (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/).

**Bottom line:** Across the single largest RCT, a Cochrane review, and multiple meta-analyses, chlorhexidine-alcohol preparation before cesarean delivery reduces SSI risk compared with iodine-alcohol, though the absolute benefit is modest and evidence certainty is moderate rather than high. This has informed clinical guidelines favoring chlorhexidine-alcohol as the preferred preoperative skin antiseptic for cesarean delivery.
